t: Minimum Number of Coins for Fruits
o: Buying fruit i (0-indexed) at prices[i] lets you take any of the next i+1 fruits free, but free fruits can also be bought to gain their own rewards. Minimize total coins to acquire all n fruits. With n ≤ 1000 an O(n²) DP suffices.
k: Let f[i] = min cost to fully acquire the first i fruits; the last acquisition event is a purchase of some fruit j whose reward covers through fruit i−1.
Buying fruit j (0-indexed) covers fruits j..2j inclusive, so f[i] = min over j with 2j+1 ≥ i of f[j] + prices[j].
Greedy doesn't work directly because cheap fruits may be worth buying for their rewards.

a.i: Every fruit is either taken free (covered by an earlier purchase) or purchased. Charging a purchase at j and requiring its coverage to reach i captures both roles: f[j] already accounts for fruits before j, and the reward spans to 2j. Taking the min over all valid last purchases yields the optimum.
s: For i from 1 to n: f[i] = min over j in [ceil(i/2)-1 .. i-1] of f[j] + prices[j] (condition 2j+1 ≥ i).
a.t: O(n²) — for each prefix we scan candidate last purchases

a.i: The candidate window lo(i) = ⌈i/2⌉−1 is non-decreasing in i, so f[i] is a sliding-window minimum of g[j] = f[j] + prices[j]. A deque keeping candidates with increasing g answers each i in O(1) — this is essentially the Hard-version solution and shows how to scale past n = 1000.
s: Deque holds indices j with increasing g[j] = f[j] + prices[j].
For each i, pop front while j < lo(i); f[i] = g at front.
Push i−1's g value (once computed) maintaining monotonicity.
a.t: O(n) — each index enters and leaves the deque once

w: Present the quadratic DP first (clear and sufficient), then the deque as the scaling trick reused in problem 2969. Pitfall: the reward of fruit j covers exactly the next j fruits (through index 2j, 0-based), off-by-one errors here are common. Verify example 3 by hand.
